nodes.plm_action: Use crimp bead pliers to clamp crimp bead
nodes.plm_caption: This video shows someone using a pair of blue and black pliers, cutting various wires and creating bracelets. The video is good quality with clear sound.

summary.brief: A craft reviewer demonstrates the Bead Buddy One‑Step Crimper while making a beaded bracelet and then talks about the tool’s ease of use.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the presenter holding the blue‑and‑black one‑step crimper and describing its three levers, including the small spring lever and the ratcheting top. She places a piece of beading wire with a crimp bead on a work surface, aligns the bead under the small lever, and squeezes the large handle to close the bead in a single motion. She repeats the process using both round and cylindrical crimp tubes, cuts away excess wire, strings additional beads, and assembles the pieces into a complete bracelet, which she shows on a plain backdrop. Throughout the demonstration an on‑screen overlay notes a “95 % success rate” and she mentions that the tool requires little hand strength and makes a good gift. After the hands‑on portion she moves to a seated setting, gestures with the pliers while speaking about the tool, and finally the video ends with end‑screen graphics promoting the Craft Test Dummies channel and a brief clip of a wire‑cutter.

action.detailed: Place a crimp bead onto the beading wire, align it under the tool’s small spring lever, then squeeze the large handle to close the bead, release, and repeat as needed to finish the bracelet.
action.actor: The female presenter (Jenny) demonstrating the crimper

nodes.plm_action: Close crimp bead so wire lays neatly in the middle of the hole
nodes.plm_caption: The video shows a woman demonstrating how to use and make jewelry. The woman starts by presenting a pair of blue and black bead buddy crimpers before putting them down on a table, and using them to crimp her own bead jewelry. A few still images of the completed bracelet are shown. Then the video closes with the woman picking up the crimpers and showing how easy they are to use.

summary.brief: Jenny reviews the Bead Buddy One‑Step Crimper, demonstrates crimping beads onto beading wire, and shows finished bracelets while noting a 95 % success rate.
summary.detailed: The video opens with Jenny introducing the blue‑and‑black Bead Buddy One‑Step Crimper, explaining its three‑lever ratcheting mechanism and placing the tool on a dark tabletop. She slides a round crimp bead onto the end of a length of beading wire, holds the bead in place with her thumb, and squeezes the large handle of the crimper so that the spring levers close the bead around the wire. She repeats the process using a cylindrical crimp tube, showing each completed crimp. Throughout she comments that the tool requires very little hand strength, that her success rate with it is about 95 %, and that it is easier to use than a regular crimping tool. She then displays several bracelets her daughter has made, highlighting how the tool lets her quickly finish the crimping while her daughter does the stringing. The segment includes a few still‑image shots of the finished bracelets and on‑screen text emphasizing the 95 % success rate. Jenny concludes by recommending the crimper as a handy, low‑effort tool and a good gift for crafters.

action.detailed: Place a crimp bead on the end of a beading wire, position it under the One‑Step Crimper’s levers, and squeeze the handles to close the bead, then repeat for additional beads.

nodes.plm_action: Thread crimp bead onto wire
nodes.plm_caption:
This video features a step by step tutorial. The tutorial displays how to make jewelry from scratch, using crimp beads.
The tutorial begins with a pair of pliers with blue handles being picked up and demonstrated in the background. Once the viewer focuses the camera, the hands pick up a wire and an earring and some crimp beads. The person displays the wire between their thumb and index fingers and uses a crimp bead to be placed on the end of the wire. The wire is bent into an open "C" and another crimp bead is placed on the end of the wire. Once the wire has been bent the crimp bead is pinched in the pliers and squeezed shut, the excess wire is cut from the pliers, the wire is pulled through to the end of the bracelet and the excess is cut and dropped to the side.

The tutorial also shows the process of making a bracelet with black and white beads. The video concludes with showing the bracelet that the viewer can potentially recreate, by displaying it on a plain white backdrop.

summary.brief: A hand uses a one‑step crimper to finish and display a beaded bracelet.
summary.detailed: The presenter picks up the blue‑handled one‑step crimping pliers, slides a crimp bead onto a length of beading wire, bends the wire into an open “C” shape, adds a second crimp bead, squeezes the pliers to close both crimps, trims the excess wire with cutters, pulls the wire through the bracelet loop and twists the tail to secure it, then strings black, white, green and blue beads (with gold spacers) onto the wire, applies a final crimp to close the loop, and holds the completed bracelet up against a plain white background.

action.detailed: Using the one‑step crimper, bend the wire, place crimp beads, squeeze to lock the crimps, cut off excess wire, twist the tail, then thread the assorted beads and finish with a final crimp, presenting the finished bracelet.
action.actor: The presenter, a woman, operating the crimping pliers and handling the beading wire

She then picks up a blue‑handled plier, threads several beads onto a dark cord, and passes the cord back and forth between her hands, pulling the strand tight. Finally, she uses the needle‑nose pliers to secure the end of the beaded strand and trim any excess, completing a tiny necklace against a dark grey background.

action.detailed: She pulls the beaded strand taut, clamps the end with needle‑nose pliers and trims the excess, completing the necklace.

llm.system_prompt:
You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to either of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   A video can match neither, one, or both. Be strict — when in doubt,
   say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.
